FINANCE
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO STUDY FINANCIAL ACTIVITIES, ENABLING LEGISLATION, ETC., OF CROWN CORPORATIONS
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, a special committee of inquiry on Crown corporations exercising financial, commercial or industrial activities be established to study the various Acts establishing such Crown corporations, the Crown Corporations Act, sections 76 to 88 of the Financial Administration Act, and all other laws concerning Crown corporations and to recommend to the House the adoption of a law regarding federal public enterprises; the committee should also study the following subjects without restrictions (a) the legal rules pertaining to the employees of such corporations (b) their financial structure (c) the way in which they are financed (d) government control over said corporations (e) fiscal regulations (municipal, school, provincial and federal taxes (f) the status of the administrators (g) the privileges of such corporations resulting from their being "commissioned by Her Majesty" (h) the status of the subsidiaries of these enterprises (i) their purchasing policy (j) the problem of auditing by the Auditor General of Canada or by private auditors (k) the appropriateness of State intervention in the economic field in the form of enterprises; and all other matters concerned.
Mr. Speaker, I apologize for presenting such a long motion, which you had to read in full because of its complexity, but you do everything so well that it is always a pleasure to hear you read those private members' motions because one feels that you consider that this hour is important.
Mr. Speaker, I have the pleasure today of coming back to a subject of great concern to me, that of Crown corporations. Since my election to this House in 1968, I have noted with astonishment the lack of interest shown by government members, especially those responsible for the Crown corporations, in the study and operation of such corporations.
I have already put on the order paper, as my colleagues well know, hundreds of questions with regard to bilingualism in the Crown corporations. Well, from the documents supplied by the government in reply to my questions. I must say that most Crown companies mock Parliament. Indeed the only link between them and Parliament, which has nevertheless established them by
legislation, is the famous annual report which in the end says nothing but commonplaces.
Mr. Speaker, in practice Crown companies have become some kind of parallel power. Generally they are government tools which act through delegated powers in some particular fields. One only has to look at the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation to readily realize the total absence of government control over these government agencies.
As for the CBC, all the minister responsible-that is the Secretary of State (Mr. Pelletier)-can do is to run errands, tell the Crown corporation what goes on in Parliament and repeat here what the Corporation has replied in answer to the complaints that we have expressed. That is all!
We cannot even criticize or discuss a reply coming from a Crown corporation. I feel that parliamentary control must be above this stupendous farce that we are presently witnessing.
That is why, is order to shed light on this matter and others related to it, in short to give details on the administration of these corporations, their usefulness and their operation, their relationships with government and Parliament, I suggest today the appointment of a special committee of inquiry, something that has never been done since the establishment of the first Crown corporation.
In the light of the comments which I would like to make, I would refer my colleagues to several studies made by university experts in that field who are especially interested in parliamentary control over institutions created by the government. My colleagues will note like myself the importance of this problem at the present time.
Mr. Speaker, when reading over the motion introduced today, we realize that I especially insist on subjects which have led me to present that motion. What are they?
I am asking in the first place the passage of a general law regarding federal public enterprises which could be used for the creation of any organization deemed necessary to meet a special need.
Mr. Speaker, at the present time there is total confusion. We cannot compare the status of Crown corporations because some are representatives of Her Majesty while others are not and in several cases there are some overlaps.
It seems to me that in a country like this one, there is no reason for not having a basic law designed to guide parliamentary control over each of those corporations without our having to be experts in their respective fields.
But before we are ready to formulate that basic law, we will naturally have to analyze exhaustively what goes on in those corporations. A special committee of inquiry is needed to that end. I ray "spec al" because I would not like it to be made only of hon. members; they should be associated with specialists and other citizens in order that a serious inquiry be made into the operations in those corporations.

June 14, 1971

That is why I ask that the committee be given terms of reference that would not be limited by legal intricacies, but that would ensure a complete study of the legal status of the employees of those corporations. This is a matter that my colleagues, in particular those who are on the front benches, would have great difficulty in understanding, because even the officials of these corporations are in doubt about it. As a matter of fact they do not understand too well the legal status of their employees. Moreover, the employees themselves find it difficult to limit, establish or defined their own legal status in the corporation.
If we ask: Are they civil servants, the Polymer Corporation will reply: We have no civil servants. Are they Crown employees? Another corporation will answer in the negative. Are they employed by the government or Parliament? Still other corporations answer in a negative way.
Mr. Speaker, it is important that the legal status of the people employed by Crown corporations be established and defined once and for all, in order that they may not only serve the public better, but also that they will know what are their status, rights and privileges.
How are Crown corporations funded? Some have shares on the market, others do not. Some issue guaranteed shares, others do not. Why? Some corporations admit the public to participation in their funding and others do not.
Mr. Speaker, this is of particular importance. There is more and more talk of establishing Crown corporations in various fields. For instance there is quite a lengthy study on the possibility of doing away with the present Post Office Department, transforming it into a Crown corporation. What, then, would be that corporation's legal status? What would be the legal status of its employees? How would it be financed? Would the public be able to participate in it? What experiences have been carried out in this field elsewhere? What are the advantages for a Crown corporation of being or of not being an agency of Her Majesty?
Mr. Speaker, there being no parliamentary study in that field members of Parliament have no guidelines in preparing and studying the legislation introduced by the government.
This committee should also study how the government and Parliament could supervise these corporations, and I am particularly interested in that.
The system of taxation is another matter we should study. It is well known, Mr. Speaker, that some Crown corporations own houses and buildings in some municipalities without having to pay any municipal, provincial or federal taxes. It is well known that some Crown corporations which are competing directly with private enterprises do not pay any taxes whereas the private enterprises are penalized, because they have to forgo part of their purchasing power in order to pay the endless number of levies, be they school, municipal, provincial or federal taxes.
Inquiry on Crown Corporations
Mr. Speaker, because the government refuses to indicate what its exact position is in this respect and to reconsider the legal status of these corporations, it unfairly competes with private enterprise. One is lead to wonder to what extent the government is consistent when it invests millions of dollars to develop private enterprise and create employment. The inconsistency is such that it would seem proper that this matter be considered exhaustively.
Another rather important question is the auditing of Crown corporations' accounts by the Auditor General of Canada. This is a vital issue that keeps coming up from time to time in this House.
Each year, in his annual report, the Auditor General complains about not having the opportunity to audit the accounts of all Crown corporations. Why is it so? The answer is very simple. It cannot be concealed. The government prefers to have the accounts of some-I should say most-Crown corporations audited by private firms. This is an undisguised form of patronage which denies Parliament direct supervision over the administration, the bookkeeping and the auditing of creatures of the government, namely, Crown corporations.
The man who represents this Parliament with Crown corporations, with departments, with the public administration is the institution known as the Auditor General of Canada. I suggest that his role should be much more extensive.
It seems to me we need a man who, within the Crown corporations and the departments, could act without restrictions, that is, who would have all the powers needed to make a full report on the bookkeeping, the financing, the working conditions of the employees and the expenditures. The government takes great care not to send the Auditor General of Canada to audit the books of those corporations, under the pretext that he does not have the time to do so. Instead of increasing judges' salaries, and salaries in other fields, we should give the Auditor General the staff required to audit those books.
Doubtless, if a special committee were set up to study the administration, the status, the financing of those corporations and the extent of the waste, we would then unanimously authorize the Auditor general to audit the books.
Every time a high official of a Crown corporation attends a meeting, even for an hour in the day, he is paid $100. I have very interesting figures on that but I do not want to bother the House with them. I would be happy to give a copy to all hon. members who would like to have one. The public does not know anything about such unbelievable waste, nor do hon. members because we do not have enough time to deal with that matter. I have given special attention to this fact and, judging by the replies to the questions I put on the Order Paper, the end result is astounding.
If we consider, for instance, the control Parliament exercises over the implementation of its adopted policy concerning bilingualism within the Public Service, it is apparent that there is none. I have actually put on the

June 14, 1971
Inquiry on Crown Corporations Order Paper question No. 53 which reads in part as follows:
What is the number of senior civil servants earning $17,000 or more a) whose mother tongue is French, b) whose tongue is English,... d) who are bilingual,

-There was nothing particularly brilliant in the following reply:
As a matter of fact, here is the reply I received:
a)	b)	c)	d)Bank of Canada	3	27	-	8Industrial Development Bank	2	20	-	3Atomic Energy of Canada Limited	-	117	3	14Eldorado Nuclear Limited Canadian Overseas	-	8	1	Telecommunication Corporation Central Mortgage and Housing	-	5	1	2Corporation	9	48	3	23
Which for six crown corporations, in the case of senior officials earning $17,000 or more, makes a total of 14 whose mother tongue is French and 225 whose mother tongue is English. That is outrageous, but we cannot do anything about it. The government is getting publicity out of its bilingualism programs and bonuses but the situation is ridiculous.
So much Mr. Speaker, for the great bilingual policy of the government. It is easy for the government to say that it has great achievements to its credit. It should also say that its policy is leading to nothing and is useless.
The Parliament has no means of control except that hon. members can put questions on the Order Paper which is quite a ridiculous method since the government gives only the information it wants to give, and it is quite often incomplete, especially when the questions relate to a Crown corporation and I will prove that later.
This is a typical example of a current and important subject, namely bilingualism, and it demonstrates, first, that the government policy in this connection is no good, difficult to implement and that its results are still to come and, secondly, that Parliament has no control over it. Since we have the information, what supervision can Parliament exercise? None practically.
Here is another example showing how important this matter is. I had put on the Order Paper the following question:
In each of the Proprietary Crown Corporations, what is the number of employees (a) who speak French only (b) who speak English only (c) who are bilingual?
Now, on September 16, 1968, the Department of Defence Production provided me with the following reply, and I quote:
As concerns the Polymer Corporation Limited: The Polymer Corporation states that among its 2,744 employees, no one speaks French only, that, to the best of their knowledge, 2,614 speak English only, whereas about 130 are bilingual.
This is a typical example of an unfortunate situation, but that is the way things are in the Public Service and in the Crown corporations. No control is being exercised. I would even say that the ministers are already overwhelmed by the creatures of which they are supposed to be responsible.
This is true, for instance, of the Secretary of State, who is totally overwhelmed by his creature, the CBC. In fact, he is unable to answer a question being asked by an hon. member, or to set the shop in order. One can see what is going on in the CBC. This is not the first time that this question is raised in the House. But we argue in a circle and get nowhere. Why? Because Parliament has no control and because the minister is not responsible for this corporation. However, under the act, he is supposed to be responsible.
Mr. Speaker, here is another example. This is another question which appeared on the Order Paper, and I
quote:
1. For each of the Proprietary Crown Corporations, what was in 1967 the return on the capital invested?
Are we not entitled, as hon. members, to wonder about such things? What is the return on the capital invested? It is important to know if the capital invested in a Crown corporation yields a profit. And, if so, to what extent?
Here is the second part of the question:
For each of the said Corporations, what was the profit in 1967 and what part of such profit was paid to the government?
What amount did the government receive? Very often Parliament votes supplies to establish such corporations. They operate and Parliament makes up the deficits. The Canadian National is a good example. We seldom hear of the reverse happening.
In any event, here is the answer which the Minister of Defence Production sent me:
With regard to the Polymer Corporation:
1.	The net income of the Corporation in 1967 equalled 5.6 per cent of the capital invested by the shareholders as of the end of the said year.
2.	The net income of the Corporation in 1967 was $5,812,000, of which $3,000,000 were paid to the government as dividends.
That is a typical case of a corporation having shown a profit and having apparently been well administered.
Now, if we compare this reply to the annual report, we find inconsistencies and may conclude that the whole thing makes no sense.
So who should we believe? I am taking a great deal of the time of the House, but I am closing my remarks with an illustration of the wide scope of the question. It is an acknowledged fact that the government owns and operates an important industrial sector...

speechtext:
I thank you, Mr. Speaker, and I also thank my colleagues. I only need two minutes at the most.
It is a recognized fact: the State owns and operates today a large industrial, commercial and financial sector.

June 14, 1971

It operates uranium mines through Eldorado Nuclear Ltd; coal mines through the Cape Breton Development Corporation. It carries out mining exploration through SOQUEM and oil exploration through Panarctic Oils Limited. It operates one of the largest railway in the world through the CNR. It owns many road transport companies controlled by the Canadian National Transportation Limited. It operates the most important hotels in Canada through the Canadian National Hotels Limited. It deals in air transport through Air Canada and Eldorado Aviation Limited and in shipping through the CNR and the Northern Transportation Co. Limited. In short, Mr. Speaker, it is an extensive and important sector.
The state is one of the world's largest rubber producers through its Polymer Corporation. It owns and operates one of the most extensive radio and television networks: the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. It produces and sells power through the Quebec and Ontario hydroelectric power commissions, and so on and so forth. It grants interest-yielding loans through the Industrial Development Bank, the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, the Farm Credit Bureau and the Deposit and Investment Fund.
In summary, Mr. Speaker, in Canada today there are over a hundred state-owned and state-operated public companies actively engaged in industrial, business and financial activities, the assets of which exceed $20 billion.
Because of the importance of this matter, I have felt justified in introducing this motion aimed at setting up a special study committee, which will shy from party politics and refrain from hustling public servants or the government, while helping to shed light upon this extensive field where over $20 billion are administered and where things are occurring that are more or less questionable or, at any rate, over which we have no control whatsoever.
In my opinion, it is in the interest of each and every member of Parliament to support this motion aimed at establishing such a committee with a view to drafting a basic piece of legislation that will guide us in the administration and management of our Crown corporations.

subtopic: FINANCE
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED ESTABLISHMENT OF SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO STUDY FINANCIAL ACTIVITIES, ENABLING LEGISLATION, ETC., OF CROWN CORPORATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had assumed that the hon. member's notice of motion probably would not be heard until after the summer recess and for that reason I had anticipated having the summer vacation to do some research on this subject because I think it is important, although the hon. member has set forth a rather tall order for a committee of this House.
I have read with considerable interest the questions that the hon. member has placed on the order paper, particularly those in connection with Polymer Corporation and the language aspect of the government's policy on bilingualism. The hon. member has seen fit once again to prove that statistics really do not mean much and that you can use them in any way you see fit. I well remember one of my colleagues talking about statistics in the House. He said that statistics are something like a bikini:
Inquiry on Crown Corporations
what they reveal is interesting, but what they conceal is vital.
The hon. member, in order to prove what he says is the case in respect of return on investment, picked the worst year Polymer has had. He mentioned it had "only" -I put "only" in quotation marks-a return of $5.3 million in profits, and he saw fit to ignore almost 15 or 20 years when profits far exceeded that figure, sometimes by two or three times as much. So the record of Polymer is a pretty splendid one and I take umbrage when the hon. member, in an attempt to prove a case, sees fit to pick out only the particular year that happens to suit his convenience.
The hon. member was speaking from a false premise when he indicated that the government was opposed to having the Auditor General examine the books or be the auditor of certain Crown corporations. That is not the case. I recall, as a member of the Public Accounts Committee, that when we were examining the role to be played by the Auditor General one of the points raised was that he should have the right to look at all Crown corporations, that he should be the auditor for all Crown corporations.
We went to the people who should know most about auditing, who should know more about it than even Members of Parliament, namely, chartered accountants and certified public accountants. As a result, I can say the government is not trying to hide anything by not having the Auditor General audit the books of Crown corporations. The corporations themselves indicated that they needed an auditor with a special kind of talent to help them in the competitive phases of their work and said that to spread the responsibilities for auditing this kind of enterprise would be doing a disservice to the Canadian taxpayer-in fact, would be doing a disservice to the people they were trying to serve. But they saw nothing wrong with the Auditor General having an investigatory role or working with auditors who have a special talent or ability to advise companies, particularly those which are involved in competitive types of business.
So, Mr. Speaker, it is not a question of the government trying to hide anything, of the government trying to conceal anything, of Crown corporations not wanting the Auditor General to participate: they were simply indicating, as did public and chartered accountants, that there are certain degrees of expertise that a particular kind of chartered accountant can bring to a corporation because of the work and study he has done on a specific subject. Therefore I take exception to the hon. member's suggestion that this is an attitude taken by the government in order to hide something. I would agree with the hon. member that there might be a role for the Auditor General to play. Perhaps some area of compromise could be found between a chartered accountant expert in the field of this particular type of corporation and the Auditor General, who has more of a supervisory and investigatory role to play in this area.
When I read the motion of the hon. member much of it seemed to make good sense, the kind of thing that maybe

June 14, 1971
Inquiry on Crown Corporations
we should be concerned with when looking at Crown corporations. I doubt whether anyone here has not had, during the time he has been a member of this House, a complaint about the CBC or a suggestion as to how it might improve its image or programming. I called my local station only last Saturday to complain about a program called "Action Alert," "Canada Alert" or "Canada Action." It seemed as though two men, well beyond the teenage stage, were trying to become Canada's oldest teenagers. One of the features had to do with advice on how to react "when the fuzz puts the finger on you." They conducted an interview with a so-called lawyer who refused to be identified because he feared he might be disbarred-and if I can ever identify him, I hope he will be disbarred

purporting to give legal advice to an individual who might be apprehended by the police.
There is nothing wrong with that kind of advice except that it is dangerous. It is instant legal advice and, Mr. Speaker, it is free legal advice, which is always subject to suspicion. In this particular case the individual made the presumption that the police are always out to get you; that if you are walking along the street smoking a cigarette they will halt you, throw you into the back of their car, haul you off to the station and in the end the judge will always believe the policeman. He made all kinds of sickening suggestions that this is the kind of way in which the police force in Canada operates. That just is not so. I will be blamed for that program by people in my riding who heard it because, first of all, they will suspect that the individual giving the advice was a lawyer. I may say that the advice he gave was pretty pathetic. But the suggestions and opinions that he delivered should not have been carried on a Crown corporation network, paid for in large measure by the taxpayers' dollar.
I think we should criticize that kind of thing, but I point out that we have the CRTC and it is to that body that we should direct our complaints. We have set up the CRTC to look into programming and the conduct of broadcasters over the airwaves. But this program incensed me so much that I called the local station directly and told them what 1 thought of it. However, it is a question of a Member of Parliament not being the final judge as to what kind of material should be carried by a Crown corporation over the airwaves. We have a body with whom we can lodge our complaints. I understand that Mr. Sid Brown, president of the police association, is in this city today and I hope he will ask for the tapes of that program and raise Cain with the CBC programming section responsible for broadcasting it on Saturday morning.
There is a role for Parliament to play in looking at Crown corporations, always being on the alert to see that they are not abusing their rights and privileges. But we !must be careful not to give the idea that there is a constant looking over the shoulders. I am thinking of corporations involved in competitive kinds of enterprises, which have the stress and strain of making business decisions and then have to account not only to shareholders but to Members of Parliament in a public forum. Surely somewhere in between a measure of control could
be exercised. Maybe it would be by studying the estimates in this House, or by raising the particular subject once in a while in this chamber.
I point out that we have the Public Accounts Committee. The Auditor General reports to us on Crown corporations that are not audited by the Auditor General. We have had representatives of four or five of these corporations appear before our committee. We have examined them with respect to the role they play, the kind of money they are spending, the profits they make or do not make and the particular service they perform. As I say, there are all kinds of opportunities available to Members of Parliament and I do not think we need worry too much about what the hon. member who moved the motion called "the parallel power."
The hon. member also dealt with the specific area involving employees of Crown corporations. It is in this area that we might have some input to contribute and on which we should spend some thought and study. Recently we heard that for a long time some people employed by the CBC were treated as civil servants and received an exemption so far as the payment of certain taxes in the United States was concerned. That exemption was subsequently withdrawn, leading to many problems, and ultimately these taxes were paid by the CBC which felt justified in paying them. This matter is still being examined by the Public Accounts Committee and a determination will be made whether in its opinion the decision made by the CBC was correct. This points up the need to look into the area involving employees of Crown corporations.
Another area I know something about is Crown corporation employees' pensions and the portability of those pensions. When an individual works for a Crown corporation and subsequently bids or tenders for a particular job with the Crown, be it in right of the province or in right of the Dominion of Canada, there should be some kind of portability of pension. That is not the case so far as all Crown corporations are concerned. As a result, an individual is not encouraged to move into government or public service when he knows that he will get a certain pension from the Crown corporation and a certain pension from the government but the combined total will be substantially less than he would have obtained had he stayed with the Crown corporation. We should not put that kind of stumbling-block in the way of individuals who want to work in the public service. I would hope something could be done to provide portability of pensions in this area.
As I indicated, Mr. Speaker, I am sorry I did not have more time to study the hon. member's motion because he has set before us a rather tall order. When I first read it the motion seemed to indicate that there was something basically wrong here. First, I think his motion is too long and, second, it is too all-encompassing. I would find it extremely difficult to support the motion in its present form.
I take exception to one other comment, Mr. Speaker, but I know other members wish an opportunity to speak.

June 14, 1971

The hon. member said that Crown corporations could not care less about Parliament. I only know about the Crown corporation because it happens to be located in my riding, but the directors invite me to go there three or four times each year, when they fill me in on what is going on. This corporation has a concern for the Member of Parliament, and the directors come here on many occasions to keep the government filled in on the kind of action they wish to take. This approach should be encouraged in all Crown corporations. I do not think it is fair to say that Crown corporations could not care less about Parliament. They are very much aware that we are here. They are created by statute which can be revoked at any time, so they are concerned. I hope the time will never come when Members of Parliament have to make the decision about what should and should not appear on a public network.

biniere (Mr. Fortin) who introduced this motion and gave the House such interesting and necessary explanations.
He also quoted some statistics relating to the francophone elements represented in various Crown corporations. I think he did it all in a very fine spirit: the hon. member did not want to make any discriminatory remarks, but he merely wanted to call the attention of the House to a situation that, unfortunately, has not received enough consideration by Parliament to have been really corrected.
I also listened very carefully to the remarks made by the previous speaker who expressed himself in very good French, and I want to congratulate him. It is a sign of goodwill on the part of the hon. members who want to co-operate to the implementation and especially the practice of bilingualism in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, in view of the interest of the situation which deserves the attention of all members of this House, the motion which has just been very briefly debated, and which should normally call for a more extended debate, is designed to show that, whatever efforts have been made in the past to ensure a fair representation of the French-speaking population of Canada, that objective has not been totally achieved. That is why, in seconding the motion, I endorse the views of the hon. member for Lotbiniere.
I am convinced that members will take the facts set forth into consideration and will co-operate heartily in order that ours may be a model country, so that all Canadians, regardless of their ethnic origin and their idiom, may have the opportunity, according to their qualifications, to fill important functions within Crown corporations.
Moreover, this motion indicates not only that the French-speaking representation leaves much room for improvement, but also that parliamentarians do not have an adequate opportunity of controlling public moneys spent by Crown corporations. A report should be given to the House and not only to committees so that each of the representatives of the people, as the hon. member who spoke before me put so well, be in a position to see how public moneys are spent, and how to attain certain goals. Has it been possible to reach the aims when Parliament decided to establish a Crown corporation?
Under the circumstances, I am very pleased to support the motion and I hope that Parliament, during the few remaining minutes at our disposal, will give its consent so that it may be agreed to.

speechtext:
I certainly appreciate the remarks that the hon. member for Hamilton-Wentworth made in the debate in both official languages. The status of Crown corporations is a complex one and is not nearly as simple as the hon. member who proposed the motion may conceive. The built-in difficulty of Crown corporations is, I suppose, inherent in the nature of the creature. You create Crown corporations because you want to create a body that is somewhat removed from political and governmental influence and control. However, sometimes things go wrong as they inevitably do. Hon. members on both sides of the House have cited examples where Crown corporations have not been as responsive as it was felt they should be, nor as accountable as it was thought they should be. They have been criticized for being independent, out of control, beyond the reach of Members of Parliament generally and of the government particularly. That, really, is the other side of the coin. That is what one bargains for when one creates an agency such as the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.
I think all of us would agree, on reflection, that it would be totally intolerable if the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation were amenable to the direct influence of the government or, for that matter, if it were affected by the day to day political whims of Parliament or individual Members of Parliament. So we pay for the independence of these agencies. We pay a certain price, and at times that price seems higher than at other times. Generally, though, I think the price is well worth paying.
Under the Financial Administration Act there are three separate classes of Crown corporations. Some Crown corporations are basically agencies of the various departments of government. They are listed in schedule B of the act and include agencies like the Agricultural Stabilization Board, the directorate of the Veterans Land Act, the Science Council and the Unemployment Insurance Commission. Those are salient examples. In schedule C there are commercial-type operations that the Crown has entered into. Under this heading we find Atomic Energy of Canada, Limited, the Canadian Dairy Commission, the Film Development Corporation and entities such as the National Capital Commission, National Harbours Board, and so on. Finally, in schedule D we have more prominent Crown corporations such as Air Canada, the CBC and Polymer Corporation that was referred to at considerable length earlier in the debate.
The Financial Administration Act requires that the capital budgets and annual reports of these corporations be laid before Parliament. I think the message of the Financial Administration Act is that the diversity of the activities and differences in the objectives of Crown corporations do not make those corporations amenable to the uniform treatment which the hon. member proposes.

Mr. Speaker, my remarks will be very brief because we have discussed this point on several occasions-second reading, in committee when we were discussing the white paper and when we were analyzing many of the briefs submitted by various organizations.
I think the hon. member's point is that under the existing unemployment insurance program the financial formula is such that the employer and the employee

June 14, 1971
Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971 share the cost and the government contributes an extra 20 per cent toward the maintenance of the unemployment insurance fund. The new concept for the future varies somewhat from this. For the first time it takes into consideration the moral obligation of the government when the rate of unemployment in this country is higher than any of us like to see. I do not think that any member of this House supports any level of unemployment. We would all like to see an utopian state where it is possible to count the number of unemployed on one hand. This does not even happen in the socialist countries of Sweden, Poland, Russia or anywhere else. It is too much to expect.
What we are in effect doing is evaluating all the opportunities of financing. We shied away from the American concept where unemployment is financed completely by employers because the employers in that country, having accepted this financial burden, have been successfull over the years in preventing any improvements to the plan. They have acted as watchdogs over the plan to the point where the plan now leaves very much to be desired.
In effect, we have developed a formula in such a way that the government will become active in the participation of the plan when the unemployment figures in this country rise above a certain level. Under the existing plan, at the present rate of unemployment the contribution of the government would be $176 million. Under the proposed plan, the contribution of the federal government will be $369 million. Everyone can see what a considerable increase this will be. Almost $200 million will come from the government coffers as the result of a rate of unemployment of 6.5 per cent. This should be, and is, an incentive for the economists of this country to control the rate of unemployment.
Why did we choose 4 per cent and not 3 per cent, 5 per cent or 6 per cent? This is not an indication that the government accepts 4 per cent as an acceptable rate of unemployment. This has happened to be the rate of unemployment over the last decade beginning with 1959 or 1960. This is not desirable. The Economic Council of Canada in their various reports have suggested 3 per cent, 3.5 per cent and 3.8 per cent. This depends on many factors, such as the birth rate and so on, which affect the rate of unemployment in this country.
The figure of 4 per cent happened to be the most practical method to determine the rate of unemployment whereby the government makes its unique contribution to the fund in the form of financial considerations. At 4 per cent the contribution of the government would be approximately what it has been over the past decade. Had 5 per cent been the figure that the contribution over the last decade had been equal to, that is the figure we would have used. Had it been 3 per cent, that is the figure we would have used. It is simply a mechanism or an indication at what level the government should assume the financial burden of the plan. It worked out at 4 per cent. Certainly at 4 per cent or 5 per cent the financial burden of the government will be approximately what it is today.
I think the financing of the plan in this way is a big improvement because it thrusts the whole burden on the
government when the rate of unemployment becomes excessive. For this reason I ask all responsible parties in the House to reject the amendment.
